sections.content:
上一序列中的代码执行了 1 个动作。
已执行动作： MOUSE(row=35, col=14).
仍在同一关卡。
当前状态：第 26 步，第 2 关。
当前有效动作：MOUSE。
唯一工具是 `python`。它提供 `current_frame`、`previous_frame`、`history`、`transitions`、`last_transition`、`valid_actions`、`last_action_result` 和 `action(actions)`。
只提供字母编码棋盘视图和轻量元数据；原始数字颜色 ID 不可用。
保持工具输出紧凑：以 `current_frame.segmentation` 为主，只用 `current_frame.ascii` 查看小块特定区域；绝不打印整盘。
最近变化应比较 `previous_frame` 与 `current_frame`，或 `last_transition.before_frame` 与 `.after_frame`；`history[-1].frame` 是当前帧，不是上一帧。
用 Python 检查证据，根据最新历史修正世界模型，并按当前理解的目标搜索或评分候选动作及短序列。
维护紧凑的工作世界模型：当前关卡包含什么、动作可能做什么、目标可能是什么、仍有哪些不确定性、什么计划最优。
下面给出上一轮的世界模型。默认复制它，再根据新证据增删内容。执行新动作前，必须先给出修订后的世界模型。
若搜索或控制循环需要，可在一段 Python 中多次调用 `action(actions)`；但结果一旦报告 `game_over`、`run_complete`、`level_completed` 或 `done`，必须立即停止。
Working world model carried from earlier turns:
- World model: each cross moves its aligned chord (or a ring) in one direction; goal = get both Y blocks into the marked slots. Probe: click top red cross once and diff.
- Plan: 2 clicks on top green cross (26,48); check completion.
- Revise any item above immediately if `current_frame` or `history` contradicts it.
世界模型结束。
聚焦 `history` 中最新变化，必要时更新目标环境变化，并区分游戏物体变化与纯 HUD 变化。
准备好后，在 `python` 内调用 `action(actions)`，执行代码选出的最佳有效动作或有序批次。找到可靠短序列时优先一次批量执行。
若搜索或控制循环需要，可在一段 Python 中多次调用 `action(actions)`。
若在工具调用前输出助手文字，应保持简短并用于更新世界模型。可选规范前缀为 `World model:`、`Goal model:`、`Action model:`、`Recent findings:`、`Open questions:`、`Plan:` 和 `Cross-level notes:`。
调用 `python` 时，只能输出本提示中为该模型规定的工具调用格式。不要添加 Markdown 代码围栏、说明文字或其他调用语法。不要把工具调用标记放进解释文字；决定调用工具后，直接输出工具调用本身。
使用 MOUSE 时，必须提供整数 row 和 col 参数。

sections.content:
Bottom red cross (35,14): chord G shifted left by one (new[i]=old[i+1]): old G=[w,S,b,w,b,S,p,b,g,S] → new G=[S,b,w,b,S,p,b,g,S,w]. Yes: added S@17, b@20, w@23, b@26, S@29, p@32, b@35, g@38, S@41, w@44; removed w@17, S@20, b@23, w@26, b@29, S@32, p@35, b@38, g@41, S@44. So bottom red = G left, same as top red = D left. The ring didn't move (only the N block in the HUD bar changed).
So all four crosses move their respective chords: red = left, green = right (probably; bottom green unverified but symmetric).
Current state:
D = [g,w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S,g] (net: D0 shifted right by 1)
G = [S,b,w,b,S,p,b,g,S,w] (G0 shifted left by 1)
D's mark (idx6) = p. G's mark (idx6) = b.
Level not yet complete. So the goal is not "both p".
Now, let me seriously think about what the goal could be.
Current marks: D=p, G=b.
Initial marks: D=g, G=p.
Hypotheses:
H1: The marks should be a specific pair (X, Y).
H2: The marks should match the color of the ring block on the same row (right side): D's row → right column D7=S; G's row → right column G7=b. So D=S, G=b.
H3: The marks should match the ring block on the same row (left side): D's row → left column D2=b; G's row → G2=b. So D=b, G=b.
H4: The two chords should be in some symmetric relationship.
H5: The marks should match the color of the cross... no, that's not it.
H6: The marks should be the color of the block at the same index on the opposite chord — that's "same color", already falsified (p,p didn't complete).
Wait, actually let me re-verify H6: when both marks were p, level_completed was False. So "same color" is falsified. OK.
H2: D=S, G=b. Currently D=p, G=b. G is already b! D needs S. D's S is at idx5 and idx8. Right shift k: (6-k) mod 10 = 5 → k=1; = 8 → k=8. So 1 top green click → D's mark=S, G's mark=b. Total 1 click!
H3: D=b, G=b. G is already b. D's b is at idx2,3. Right shift: (6-k) mod 10 = 2 → k=4; = 3 → k=3. So 3 top green clicks.
Hmm, H2 is 1 click, H3 is 3 clicks. If the goal is H2, then 1 top green click completes it. If H3, then 3 clicks.
Which is more likely as the designer's intent? "The chord block in the marked slot should match the color of the ring block on the same row" — the marked slot is at c35, the right ring column is at c38, the left is at c23. The marked slot is between them, but closer to the right (3 columns vs 12 columns). Hmm.
Actually wait. Let me reconsider. The marked slot is at c35-36. The chord cells are c17, 20, 23, 26, 29, 32, 35, 38, 41, 44. The ring columns are c23 (left) and c38 (right). The marked slot (c35) is right next to the right column cell (c38). So the marked slot is "the cell adjacent to the right ring column". The designer's intent might be: "the chord block next to the right ring should match the ring block".
Or, the intended goal might be something entirely different. Let me look at the image again. In the current image: D's row: gray, white, blue, blue, white, sky, [mark: purple], gray, sky, gray. G's row: sky, blue, white, blue, sky, [mark: blue], gray, sky, white... wait, let me re-read from the image: G's row: sky (17), blue (20), white (23), blue (26), sky (29), blue (32)?? Hmm, the image shows: G's row: S, b, w, b, S, b, [mark], S, w? Let me trust the diff: G = [S,b,w,b,S,p,b,g,S,w] — wait, the diff showed added p@32 and b@35. So G: S@17, b@20, w@23, b@26, S@29, p@32, b@35, g@38, S@41, w@44. Mark (c35) = b. In the image the marked cell looks blue — yes.
Hmm, OK, another thought — what if the goal is that the marked slot should hold the color of the ring block diagonally above/below it? The marked slot is at (26-27, 35-36). The ring's right column is at c38-39: D7=(26-27, 38-39)=S. The marked slot is adjacent (c36 touches c38? no, c36 and c38 — there's a gap at c37... the chord pitch is 3: c35-36, then c38-39. So the marked slot c35-36 is directly adjacent to the right column cell c38-39 (sharing an edge at c37? c36+1=c37, c38 — no, c37 is between them, so not adjacent, 1 column gap).
I keep going in circles. Let me think about the puzzle from the designer's perspective. Level 1: ring rotation, bring the unique Y to the marked slot. Level 2: two chord tracks. The marked slots are on the chords. The unique block on each chord is p. I brought both p's to the marked slots — not complete. So the designer's goal is not "p to the slot".
What if the goal is the opposite: the marked slot should not hold p? That is, "move p out of the marked slot"? Initially D's mark=g (not p), G's mark=p (is p!). So the goal might be: G's mark ≠ p (move p out), and D's mark = something? Hmm, weird.
What if the goal is: the marked slot should hold the color of the block at the left end of the chord (the cell adjacent to the red cross)? D's left end is currently g, G's left end is currently S. Goal: D's mark=g (already! D's mark=p, no wait D's mark=p, left end=g. Not equal). Hmm: D's mark=p, D's left end=g; G's mark=b, G's left end=S.
What if the goal is: the marked slot should hold the color of the block at the right end (adjacent to the green cross)? D's right end=g (idx9), G's right end=w (idx9). Goal: D=g, G=w? Currently D=p, G=b. D's g is at idx0,7: right shift (6-k) mod 10=7 → k=9; =0 → k=6. Left shift: (6+k) mod 10 = 7 → k=1; =0 → k=4. Minimum 1 top red! G's w is at idx2,9: right shift (6-k) mod 10 = 9 → k=7; =2 → k=4. Left shift: (6+k) mod 10=9 → k=3; =2 → k=6. Minimum 3 bottom reds. Total 4 clicks. Hmm.
Too many candidate goals. I need a better approach: think about what's special/unique about the initial configuration.
Initial D0 = [w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S,g,g], G0 = [w,S,b,w,b,S,p,b,g,S].
Initial marks: D=g, G=p.
Notice: D0[6]=g and G0[6]=p. The marked slot holds g and p. p is the unique color on both chords. g: D has g×2, G has g×1.
What if the goal is: the marked slot should hold the color that appears exactly once on that chord (p) — already falsified.
What if the goal is: the two marked slots should hold the colors that appear exactly once on the opposite chord? D's mark = G's unique = p; G's mark = D's unique = p. That's "both p" — falsified.
What if the goal is: the marked slot of each chord should hold the color of the corresponding cross... the crosses are red/green. No.
Let me look at the ring more carefully. Maybe the ring blocks are the "targets": the chord block in the marked slot should match the ring block at a specific position. The ring has R (left, 2 of them), N (right, 2 of them), Y (top, 1; left, 1). The ring blocks adjacent to the marked slot: right column D7=S (same row as D's mark), right column G7=b (same row as G's mark).
H2 (D=S, G=b) is 1 click from now (1 top green). Let me reconsider: is there any other interpretation that's 1 click?
- D's mark=S, G's mark=b: 1 top green.
- D's mark=g (back to initial), G's mark=b: D's g is at idx0,7 → 1 top red (k=1: (6+1) mod 10=7=g). So 1 top red makes D's mark=g, G's mark=b. That's "D back to initial, G shifted left by 1". Weird goal.
Hmm, what if the goal is simply: the marked slot should match the ring block on the same row on the right side (H2)? That's a clean rule: "each chord's marked cell should match the ring cell on the same row on the right side". And the solution: D: S is at idx4,7 → right shift k: (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {4,7} → k=2 or 9 → 2 top greens; G: b is at idx2,4,7 → left shift k: (6+k) mod 10 ∈ {2,4,7} → k=6, 8, 1 → 1 bottom red. Total from initial: 3 clicks. From now: D's mark is p, S is at idx5,8 → 1 top green; G is already b → 0. Total 1 click.
Or the left-side version (H3): D=b, G=b: from now: D's b is at idx2,3 → 3 top greens (k=3: (6-3)=3=b); G is already b → 0. 3 clicks.
I have to decide. Actually, let me reconsider the whole thing. Maybe the goal is not about matching the ring at all. Let me think about symmetry: the board is left-right symmetric in structure (red cross on the left, green cross on the right, ring on both sides). The marked slot is at c35, slightly right of center (center is c32.5? The chord spans c17-c44, center = c30.5; the mark is at c35, which is right of center). Hmm, the mark is not at the center.
Wait, let me actually recompute: chord cells c17, 20, 23, 26, 29, 32, 35, 38, 41, 44. Center between c32 and c35. The marked slot is at c35 (idx6). The ring columns are at c23 (idx2) and c38 (idx7). So the marked slot (idx6) is adjacent to the right ring column (idx7).
Design intent: "the chord cell next to the right ring column should match the ring column block on the same row". That's H2. I think H2 is the most geometrically natural: the marked slot is the chord cell adjacent to the right ring, and the goal is to make it match the ring block on the same row.
But honestly, I'm not confident. Let me consider the cost of trying H2: 1 top green click. If it completes → done. If not, I've spent 1 click and can try H3 (2 more top greens to make D=b... wait, from the state after 1 green, D's mark=S; to make D=b: b is at idx3,4 → right shift (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {3,4} → k=3,2 → 2 more greens). So worst case H2→H3: 3 clicks total, same as direct H3.
Actually, a smarter order: first try H3 directly? H3 = 3 top greens. If H2 is the goal, after 3 greens D's mark = ? D is currently [g,w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S,g]; 3 right shifts: new[6] = D[3] = b. So after 3 greens: D's mark=b, G's mark=b. If H2 (D=S, G=b) is the goal → not complete, and I've spent 3 clicks; then D's S is at... after 3 greens D = [S,g,w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S]... let me not go down this path.
Better: try H2 first (1 click). If it completes, great. If not, I know the goal is not (S,b), and I can continue.
But wait — before spending a click, let me think if there's a way to infer the goal without a click.
Let me look at the initial configuration again: D0's mark=g, G0's mark=p. Under H2 the goal is (S,b): D needs 2 greens (or 9 reds), G needs 1 red (or 9 greens) → 3 clicks from initial. Under H3 the goal is (b,b): D needs 3 greens (or 7 reds), G needs 1 red → 4 clicks. Under "both p": D needs 1 green, G needs 0 → 1 click from initial! But I did 1 red + 2 greens = net 1 green on D, and 0 on G — that's exactly the "both p" state from the initial solution, and it didn't complete. So "both p" is definitively falsified (I was in that exact state).
Hmm wait, was I really? Initial D0, 1 net right shift: D = [g,w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S,g] — mark (idx6) = p ✓. G0 unchanged — mark = p ✓. Yes, I was in the "both p" state. Not complete. Falsified.
So the goal requires at least some movement of G (since G's mark=p in the initial state, and "both p" failed... unless the goal is D=p, G=non-p).
Candidate goals with minimal solution from initial:
- H2 (S,b): 3 clicks (D: 2 greens, G: 1 red).
- H3 (b,b): 4 clicks (D: 3 greens, G: 1 red).
- (g,b): D: 0 (initial g), G: 1 red → 1 click. But then the goal is "D stays g, G becomes b" — asymmetric and weird, and D's initial mark is already g.
- (p, non-p): D: 1 green, G: 1 red → 2 clicks. "D's mark=p, G's mark≠p"? Weird.
- (S,p): D: 2 greens, G: 0 → 2 clicks. "D=S, G stays p"? Also asymmetric.
- (w,w): D: 4 greens (w is at idx0,3: (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {0,3} → k=6,3 → 3 greens! Wait: D0's w is at idx0,3. Right shift k: new[6]=D0[(6-k) mod 10]. (6-k) mod 10=0 → k=6; =3 → k=3. So 3 greens. G0's w is at idx0,3: same → 3 greens. Total 6 clicks.
- (S,S): D0's S is at idx4,7: (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {4,7} → k=2,9 → 2 greens. G0's S is at idx1,5,9: (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {1,5,9} → k=5,1,7 → 1 green. Total 3 clicks! (D: 2 greens, G: 1 green.)
- (b,b): D0's b is at idx1,2: (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {1,2} → k=5,4 → 4 greens... wait, I said 3 earlier. Let me recompute: D0 = [w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S,g,g]: b is at idx1,2. Right shift k: new[6] = D0[(6-k) mod 10]. (6-k) mod 10 = 1 → k=5; = 2 → k=4. So 4 greens (or left shift: (6+k) mod 10 ∈ {1,2} → k=5,6 → 5 reds). So D needs 4 greens. G0's b is at idx2,4,7: (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {2,4,7} → k=4,2,9 → 2 greens. Total (b,b): 4+2 = 6 clicks. Hmm, I miscalculated earlier.
Let me redo all the minimal costs from initial (right shift = green, left shift = red; cost = min(k_right, 10-k_right)):
D0 = [w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S,g,g] (idx0-9), mark=idx6.
G0 = [w,S,b,w,b,S,p,b,g,S], mark=idx6.
For each color, D's cost to mark:
- w (idx0,3): right k: (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {0,3} → k=6,3 → min 3. Left k: (6+k) mod 10 ∈ {0,3} → k=4,7 → min 4. → 3.
- b (idx1,2): right: k=5,4 → 4. Left: k=5,6 → 5. → 4.
- S (idx4,7): right: k=2,9 → 2. Left: k=8,1 → 1. → 1!
- p (idx5): right: k=1. Left: k=9. → 1.
- g (idx6,8): right: k=0,8 → 0. Left: k=0,2 → 0. → 0 (initial).
G0:
- w (idx0,3): right: k=6,3 → 3. Left: k=4,7 → 4. → 3.
- S (idx1,5,9): right: k=5,1,7 → 1. Left: k=9,5,1... (6+k) mod 10 ∈ {1,5,9} → k=5,9,3 → 3. → 1.
- b (idx2,4,7): right: k=4,2,9 → 2. Left: k=6,8,1 → 1. → 1.
- p (idx6): 0.
- g (idx8): right: k=8. Left: k=2. → 2.
So the minimal costs from initial:
- (S,b): D 1 (red), G 1 (red) → 2 clicks!
- (S,S): D 1, G 1 → 2 clicks!
- (p, anything): D 1...
- (g,b): D 0, G 1 → 1 click.
- (g,S): D 0, G 1 → 1 click.
- (p,b): D 1, G 1 → 2 clicks.
- (p,S): D 1, G 1 → 2 clicks.
- (w,w): 3+3=6. (b,b): 4+2=6. (g,g): 0+2=2.
Hmm, many 2-click candidates. The designer's solution is probably short (level 1 was 5 clicks). Candidates with total 2: (S,b), (S,S), (p,b), (p,S), (g,g).
Now, which is most "natural"?
- (S,S): both marks sky blue. Hmm.
- (S,b): D=sky, G=blue.
- (g,g): D stays g, G becomes g.
- (p,b), (p,S): D=p (unique block to slot!), G=something.
Oh wait. What if the goal is: D's mark = p (unique block to slot, like level 1) AND G's mark = the color of the ring block on the same row on the right side (b)? That's (p,b) = 2 clicks from initial. Hmm, but that's a mixed rule.
Or: the goal is: D's mark = p AND G's mark = S? (p,S): 2 clicks. Why S? G's row, right column G7=b, left column G2=b. Not S.
Or: the goal is: the marked slot should match the ring block on the same row on the right side: D's row → D7=S, G's row → G7=b → (S,b): 2 clicks from initial (D: 1 red, G: 1 red). Clean rule, 2 clicks.
Or: the marked slot should match the ring block on the same row on the left side: D2=b, G2=b → (b,b): 6 clicks.
Hmm, (S,b) via the right-side rule is elegant: 2 clicks, clean geometric rule. And interestingly, the marked slot is adjacent to the right ring column.
But wait, why would the designer mark a slot adjacent to the right column and require matching the right column? Because the marked slot is the chord cell closest to the right ring column. The rule "the chord cell next to the right ring should match the ring block on the same row" is geometrically natural.
Alternatively, the rule might be "the marked slot should match the ring block on the same row on the right side" — same thing.
Let me also consider: the rule might involve the Y blocks: the Y at A5 (top row) and the Y at H2 (left column). The Y at A5 is in the top row at c32-33 (idx4 of the top row: R,S,b,p,Y,p,N). The Y at H2 is in the left column at r38-39. Hmm, what do these indicate? Maybe the Y blocks are just decorative "you are here" markers... or maybe they indicate the target color for the marked slot: the color adjacent to the Y? The Y at A5 is adjacent to p,p. The Y at H2 is adjacent to b (G2) and g (I2). Mixed.
I think the right-side ring matching (S,b) is my best hypothesis. From the current state (D = D0 right 1 = [g,w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S,g], G = G0 left 1 = [S,b,w,b,S,p,b,g,S,w]):
- D's mark = p. To make it S: D's S is at idx5,8. Right shift: (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {5,8} → k=1,8 → 1 green. Left shift: (6+k) mod 10 ∈ {5,8} → k=9,2 → 2 reds. → 1 top green.
- G's mark = b. Already b ✓. 0 clicks.
So: 1 top green click. If (S,b) is the goal → complete!
If not complete, the next candidates: (S,S): G needs S: G's S is at idx0,8: right shift (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {0,8} → k=6,8 → 6; left shift (6+k) mod 10 ∈ {0,8} → k=4,2 → 2 reds. So 2 bottom reds (total 3). (p,b): D is already p, G is already b — that's the current state, already falsified (not complete). (p,S): G needs S → 2 bottom reds (total 3). (g,g): D needs g: D's g is at idx0,7: right shift (6-k) mod 10 ∈ {0,7} → k=6,9 → 6; left shift (6+k) mod 10 ∈ {0,7} → k=4,1 → 1 red. G needs g: G's g is at idx7: left shift (6+k) mod 10=7 → k=1 → 1 red. So (g,g): 1 top red + 1 bottom red = 2 more clicks (total 3).
Plan: click top green once. Check. If not complete, click bottom red once (→ (S,S) or (p,S) or (g? no...)). Hmm wait, after 1 top green: D's mark=S, G's mark=b. Then:
- If the goal is (S,b) → complete.
- If the goal is (S,S): need G=S → 2 bottom reds (or 6 greens).
- If the goal is (p,S): need D=p again → 1 top red (back to current D) + G=S 2 reds.
- If the goal is (g,g): need D=g (1 red) and G=g (1 red).
- If the goal is (b,b): D=b: 3 greens... etc.
Let me just try 1 top green first. Actually, wait — let me reconsider whether the goal could be (S,b) via the left-side rule... the left-side rule gives (b,b). The right-side rule gives (S,b). The marked slot is adjacent to the right column → right-side rule → (S,b).
Hmm, one more consideration: maybe the rule is "the marked slot should match the ring block on the same row on the side of the green cross" (right side) — consistent.
Also, let me double-check the ring block colors on the same row: right column (c38-39): A7=N (17), B7=b (20), C7=S (23), D7=S (26), E7=w (29), F7=g (32), G7=b (35), H7=w (38), I7=b (41), J7=? (44). From the initial segmentation: node 18 N(17,38), 19 b(20,38), 20 S(23,38), 21 S(26,38), 22 w(29,38), 26 g(32,38), 36 S(26,38)?? Wait, node 36 is S(26,38) area 4 — that's D7=S. And node 60 b(35,38) = G7=b. Yes: D7=S, G7=b. ✓.
So the plan: 1 top green click (26,48). Check level_completed.

World model update:
- Bottom red (35,14) = shift chord G left (verified, same rule as top red). Ring static; only HUD bar changed. So: red crosses = left shift, green = right shift, each on its own chord.
- Current: D=[g,w,b,b,w,S,p,g,S,g] (marked=p), G=[S,b,w,b,S,p,b,g,S,w] (marked=b). "Both p" state was reached and NOT complete → falsified.
- New leading hypothesis: marked slot (chord cell adjacent to right ring column) must match the ring block in its row: D7=S, G7=b → target (D=S, G=b). G already b. D needs 1 green click (S at idx5 → right shift 1).
- Fallbacks if not complete: (S,S) or (p,S) → 2 bottom reds; (g,g) → 1 top red + 1 bottom red; (b,b) → more greens.

<parameter=code>
def chord(f,row):
    L=f.ascii.split('\n'); return [L[row][c] for c in (17,20,23,26,29,32,35,38,41,44)]
action([{'action':'MOUSE','row':26,'col':48}])
print("D:",chord(current_frame,26),"G:",chord(current_frame,35))
print({k:last_action_result.get(k) for k in ('board_changed','level_completed','game_over','done','run_complete')})
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
